4. Psychological report on the personality of the Servant of God, made by Prof. Sante Bidoli of S. Donà di Piave (Venice), dated 1 May 1989.

The report is made with the psychodiagnostic personality test of the Psychology of handwriting and the T.A.P.S. on psychopathologies. The intensity of aptitudes and tendencies is evaluated according to the following scale of values: Nil Slight - Appreciable - Relevant - Marked - Considerable - Strong - Maximum.

INTELLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE

The general picture of the intelligence, of a predominantly intuitive type, indicates an orientation toward the concrete and creativity markedly above the common average. Capacity for abstraction is also good, but inadequate in relation to the other intellective gifts: from this derives the need to conform to social schemes corresponding to one's own ideals, which turn out to be considerably high.

In detail, the assimilative process rests on a strong confidence in one's own mental means: the intensity of attention is considerable and its speed very strong.

It is distributed in an equally considerable measure both in the practical field and in the field of ideality, with a maximum regularity. This was disturbed in the younger age by a slight excess of rigidity, later disappeared, and by appreciable distractibility by appearances and formal aesthetics.

As regards assimilation and a first elaboration of things learned, abstraction turns out good, recognition is based on a medium capacity for comparison and on an almost maximum discernment, while interpretation rests on a panoramic view of breadth which varied over time. In the young years it was reduced, but later became much broader and adequate to the subject's needs; in the interpretation of reality the elements are linked together to a considerable degree and are strongly coordinated. One might say that the initially fideistic attitude later became also rational.

Memory presents a very strong capacity for classification, especially for facts and knowledge of an affective and moral order. The retention of these contents is maximum.

Mode of operation of the automatisms

The automatisms operate in her with almost maximum precision, strong practicality and quickness. A strong instinct to arrive at the concrete without wasting time, with considerable economy of means, is also found.

DEGREE OF KNOWLEDGE OF REALITY

The subject's mentality is characterized by maximum capacity to grasp nuances, but is not free from prejudices, both through a relevant tendency to overvalue passionately one's own way of thinking, and through the tendency to let oneself be seized by pessimism in phases of depression.

The mind presents factors of ductility through considerable mental yielding before the pressures of the environment, but also a very strong tenacity in one's own ideas which reaches obstinacy in order to obtain what she considers necessary and useful.

Mental clarity is considerable.

Real objectivity is characterized by scant depth (in youth, the depth was much greater), but also by strong capacity to grasp detail and to realize the essential of things and situations.

A marked excess of sensitivity for idealisms and a slight one for material elements disturb objectivity.

In sum, the capacity to grasp reality is oriented by ideals which are predominantly social, anchored to a transcendent reality to which the subject attributes the value of certainty.

MODE OF ELABORATING REALITY

Appreciably above the common average is mental aggressiveness regarding ideas of knowledge; marked the drive toward the new and the tendency to make variations on known themes, with uncommon, slightly whimsical tonalities.

The psyche tends to present its own productions to the environment with an appreciable pressure of an intrusive type, yet free from utopianism, acceptable with some insistence on the part of the environment itself. This attitude appeared in an evolutionary phase, compared with the youthful attitude of passive and rigid collaboration with the environment itself.

SENSITIVITY TO OTHERS' INSIDIOUS INTENTIONS

An appreciable diffidence, which in the younger age was largely hidden, puts her on the alert before others' behavior. A relevant suspiciousness produced by hypersensitivity subsequently sets in.

Suspicion provokes in her a medium tendency to investigate, supported however by considerable psychological intuition. Scant is the sensitivity in grasping disloyal and astute actions; better that in grasping creeping, amoral and insincere actions. In substance she is not very skillful in grasping others' insidious intentions, which justifies the diffidence and suspiciousness that turn out a little above the common average.

She tends, however, to revise her view through impulses to a maximum generosity in considering the motives of others' actions and through considerable mental yielding, but not always when personal matters are concerned: a strong critical sense matured with age and a strong touchiness and obstinacy tend instead to oppose rectifications.

PERSONALITY

DEGREE OF EMOTIVITY

Sensing more or less well others' insidious intentions regarding herself, she feels indignation and very strong emotions with marked sensations of anxiety and anguish, but with medium worry.

Afterward, differently from what happened in the young age, the subject manages to frame the situation with strong realism and tends toward clarification with the adversary through very strong impulses of frankness and strong impetuosity, yet is somewhat restrained by marked impressionability and driven to seek the support of influential persons to overcome the difficulties of conflict.

The maximum delicacy, the marked hypersensitivity, the considerable touchiness and resentment provoke, according to place and circumstances, impulses of anger that would express themselves with strong impetuosity, considerable irritability through excess of psychonervous tension and considerable aggressive fieriness if self-control did not intervene.

Despite a marked tendency to keep calm, the peripheral and central nervous brakes are not sufficiently effective.

Centro-associative self-mastery presents a good efficiency thanks to the strong contribution of intelligence, of the view of things in a broad picture and of self-discipline.

To the action of the brakes is added the inhibiting action of a certain sense of inferiority through fear of inconveniencing others: anger is therefore dominated or expressed under the control of intelligence in a manner adequate to the subject's psychic needs and purposes of action. The reaction therefore serves, to a considerable degree, to correct and improve personal relations, making them more realistic.

Afterward, a considerable love of concord, the maximum generosity already recalled in considering the motives of others' actions, a considerable sorrow at seeing others saddened by facts in which she has had a part, a considerable affective nostalgia, drive the subject to reconciliation, of which she takes the initiative, with strong intensity and frequency.

She grants with considerable ease forgiveness to offenders and satisfaction to the offended, refusing, to a strong degree, to demand satisfaction or to put desires of revenge into act.

AFFECTIVITY

In choosing the persons to admit to her conversation, friendship and intimacy, the subject feels considerable repugnance toward persons who neglect personal presentation and very strong repugnance toward those who do not correspond to her ethical requirements. She also has touches of shyness which, however, hardly emerge.

The psychological means she uses to establish affective relations consist of strong sympathy, maximum expansiveness, strong effusion and considerable confidentiality. Such means are supported by a considerably brilliant conversation.

The affections turn out strongly essential and respectful of others' personality; they are felt with a maximum delicacy, but not with great depth, so that the subject hardly attaches herself to one person, tending to extend the expression of her affectivity to the group rather than to the individual. They are manifested with delicacy, effusion, expansiveness and confidentiality and moreover with strong essentiality, considerable understanding, impetus, affective warmth and tenderness and with a marked ease in being moved to tears.

The drives of sexuality turn out appreciably above the average in the younger age, on the average in the age considered. A very strong tendency to sublimation and a mental refusal to deal with subjects of a sexual nature are however noted. Nevertheless in fantasy there are «temptations» which however do not prove operative.

The sense of motherhood is considerable.

The subject is much inclined to educational activity, through considerable psychological understanding and adaptability to the mentality and sentiment of children. One also notes, but only occasionally, much ease in joining in their games.

ETHICAL-RELIGIOUS SENTIMENT

The attitude toward the neighbor is characterized by considerable understanding and complacency, by maximum generosity and by very considerable respect for others' freedom. These elevated altruistic drives are contrasted and made difficult to practice by a considerable tendency to refuse sacrifice, even her own share. The contrast does not succeed in restraining these drives, yet it burdens the practical action of helping others, making it tiring for the subject. The overall attitude of the personality toward the neighbor turns out predominantly altruistic to excess.

p. 899

The attitude toward herself is characterized by considerable capacities of adaptation, pliancy and submission, by strong modesty and by a marked sense of democracy. There also operate, however, a modest pride with slight touches of exasperation and shyness, a strong sense of decorum and dignity and an appreciable haughtiness together with a marked ambition as aspiration to create things useful to the neighbor.

In the personality there are present passional drives due to strong irascibility and affectivity and to strong avidity for enjoyment of life (passionality of impetus). The stiffening passionalities, tied to pride, are on the other hand more reduced than the common average.

The extratensive passions consist of modest desires for revenge, the fruit of the painfulness provoked by others' attitude, which the person is very far from putting into act, and of an appreciable tendency to prodigality.

Intratensive passions of envy and jealousy are also noted, which are however attenuated by generosity and above all kept well in check by a strong self-discipline.

The psychic energy is free of volitional and moral limpness, so that there is a strong containment of the expansive drives of the personality with a good margin of safety.

The religious sensibility turns out reinforced by an elevated mystical tendency and by an ascetic taste of a sacrificial type aimed at conquering the intratensive passions.

The ethical sensibility is realized through a maximum rectitude, a more than considerable love of clear actions and a maximum repugnance for illegitimate affections. Some drives to scrupulosity through appreciable anxiety are noted.

The subject also feels strong impulses toward her own intellectual, sentimental and volitional perfecting.

PSYCHOPATHOLOGICAL ANALYSIS (FROM THE TAPS)

A background anxiety emerges, due mainly to the education received in childhood and to social pressures. The educational action toward her was passional and aggressive rather than rigid and produced some blocks in psychosexual evolution and a marked aggressiveness toward the environment.

From this derived a mental orientation of defense against the family and society, seen as a source of suffering, yet without destructive intents except in relation to what is considered malevolent. Rather there prevails a revolutionary aggressiveness, constructive for the human being, with a passional but positive ideal of good.

Regressive (or schizoid) tendencies are scant and paranoid ones also reduced, although an appreciable background sense of persecution accompanies her throughout life, a source of the appreciably excessive anxiety noted in the preceding analysis. There are some barely detectable mental blocks (residue of family education), while the relation with the maternal figure seems to have been sufficiently good and affectively gratifying.

The strong passionality of impetus, the intratensive one and, at the same time, the high capacities of self-control over them are confirmed.

The psychic background turns out therefore fundamentally sound; capable of dominating some non-excessive neurotic tendencies, which are directed positively toward solutions useful for herself and for the environment.

BEHAVIORS, INTERESTS, APTITUDES

The relation with reality has become broader with time, allowing her to control the strong impetus and the avidity for enjoyment of all aspects of life.

Her mood is usually considerably cheerful and is for the most part strongly moderate and decorous, although childlike manifestations and some slight whimsy sometimes emerge; at other times states of depression emerge accompanied by slight shyness and by somatic rather than behavioral resonances, behavior being characterized by strong balance. The capacity for recovery is very strong.

Almost strong is the sense of awareness and responsibility.

Considerable the impulses to enjoy the sensory world, strong those to draw satisfactions from affectivity and industriousness. The subject's tastes are refined to an almost strong degree, entrusted to a good substantial sensibility, superior to a relevant degree to the common average and characterized by considerable demands of formal correctness.

They are directed toward aesthetics and order, with a marked artistic sense both creative and critical.

Strong are the philosophical and humanistic interests directed in a concrete and scientific way toward the socio-political and historical world; medium the administrative and economic interests.

In expenditure the subject tends to balance to a considerable degree, oscillating however between a maximum drive to be lavish and a relevant tendency to provident accumulation. Balance in expenditure therefore arises from a rational search between opposite impulses.

DELIBERATIVE CAPACITIES

In the organization of groups in which the subject can express her creativity concretely, the ideas are very valid and realistic. In evaluating possible insidious intentions of others, objectivity is good when it is a matter of defending the group to which she belongs, while it is more reduced when only personal defense is at stake.

Ideas flow to memory with strong speed and marked freedom from haste. A maximum capacity is found to drive from the field of consideration ideas that have no bearing on the object to be decided, despite occasional interference of an appreciable passionality.

The basic cognitive structures for deliberation are therefore inadequate for the defense of the personality, but more than valid when it is a matter of safeguarding the interests of a social group in which she is inserted.

The aims of the useful-pleasurable are oriented in an expansive form toward enjoyment and love of life.

The altruistic drives are set predominantly in an ethical sense, with a strong sense of duty and high moral sensibility and self-discipline.

The altruistic impulses and those directed to the enjoyment of life turn out harmonized to a considerable degree, so as to determine an activity at once profitable for the person and for the environment.

In the balance of forces between herself and the environment she oscillates between overvaluation and undervaluation, while in evaluating the resistances of external reality she generally presents a very strong realism, which however sometimes reduces greatly (perhaps in concomitance with fideistic surges).

The subject, in coordinating the elements of the various variants of action examined in the course of deliberation, makes use of considerable logic, strong practicality, order and precision. Deliberations are disturbed by a slight excess of the sense of responsibility.

DECISION -

The subject, in setting the aims of action, makes use of an initiative that collaborates to a strong degree with the environmental reality, with a slight tendency to force it, and is capable of finding original solutions and of adapting to the need of others' suggestions.

Decisions are prompt to a strong degree. Their resoluteness is considerable, except when it is a matter of inconveniencing the neighbor. They exercise on others' will an average energy. When energy weakens it is replaced by a strong dynamism.

Decisions are consistent to a considerable degree.

Courage is in her contradictory: on one side are found a strong panoramic vision of the circumstances and consequences of decisions, with a strong firmness in facing adversities, adequate to the person's psychic dynamics; on the other, an excess of nervous sensitivity and emotivity would render her indecisive. A boldness sets in that overcomes her own hesitations when she must face tasks and decisions she feels to be beyond her strength.

i

Very strong is the capacity for self-criticism. Self-rectification, on the other hand, is not adequate to self-criticism: modifying her own decisions costs the subject much effort.

Perseverance results from the combination of strong tenacity and obstinacy, considerable affective and nostalgic attachment to one's own ideas and purposes, strong sense of duty.

CAPACITY FOR ACTION

Initiative is slightly above the common average, with the characteristics already described on p. 14. Action on things shows strong dynamism, maximum vigor and considerable elasticity, but also considerable rigid tension. She exhausts all initiatives to a strong degree.

Action on persons is generally exercised with medium imperiousness, which however she uses only when she considers it necessary. What acts rather, to a relevant degree, is the dynamic factor of enterprise and aggressiveness, considerable aggressive fieriness and strong impetuosity.

The conceptual and psychological contents of command are above the common average to a relevant degree. The affective content is very strong through impetuosity, generosity, warmth, impetus, tenderness and delicacy.

The subject is moreover endowed to a considerable degree with sensitivity for the psychological situation of the persons over whom she exercises command and with considerable tact, which expresses itself in gentle, cordial and optimistic ways.

The capacity to impose oneself is therefore strongly efficient through the aptitude for winning the feelings and persuading the intelligence, rather than exercising coercion on others' will.

The action of the will on her own personality is strong through strong self-discipline and the sense of duty.

DEFENSE OF ONE'S OWN PURPOSES AND DECISIONS

External defense against the oppositions of the environment is generally weak. Sometimes, however, attitudes of exasperation emerge if the oppositions are unreasonable.

Internal defense, on the other hand, is obstinate.

The subject therefore yields momentarily before hardly surmountable obstacles, setting aside her purposes while waiting for the oppositions to weaken, in order to realize them later; or seeks to obtain the support of persons who can influence the situation in the desired sense.

SITUATION IN THE LAST PERIOD OF LIFE (1900)

The letter of April 1900 shows a person physically debilitated, but still psychologically very dynamic and aware. The situation is the same as 10 years earlier, with an increase of the drives to generosity and to positively operative expansion toward the environment, although both the volitional pressure and the forces for realization are by now completely lacking.

S. Donà di Piave, 1.5.1989.

To the Most Illustrious and Reverend

Monsignor Salvatore Natucci

Promoter General of the Faith

News concerning the writings of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, in the part regarding the book entitled «Labors and Consolations of the soul on the way of perfection described by a Servant of God».

It is well to premise that the undersigned knew the Servant of God from 1874 or 1875, when he was still a layman in Naples, and he knew her through the fact that, the Servant of God having come to Naples to make a foundation there, she was entrusted by Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, Archbishop of Naples, of holy memory, to Princess of Belmonte, mother of the undersigned, to be helped in her holy purpose, and since the undersigned amused himself a little with painting, the same Most Eminent Cardinal said to Mama: «the picture for the Chapel Gennarino can do».

A few years later the writer enrolled in the Clergy of Naples, was subsequently ordained, and as soon as he was a Priest the spiritual care of the Daughters of St. Anne in Naples was entrusted to him by Cardinal Sanfelice, of venerated memory.

From that time the Servant of God had an unlimited trust in the undersigned, who, although he was never her confessor, was nevertheless made party to everything concerning the spirit of the Servant of God, and also the affairs of the Institute.

In 1893 the undersigned moved to Rome as attached to the Secretariat of State.

Among the communications of spirit of the Servant of God was that of making the undersigned party to the trials and privileges that Jesus granted her, of which the Servant of God daily took note, making as it were an account of her life, a thing known to no one, done with great reluctance on her part, willed by Him who can do all that He wills, and also encouraged by the undersigned, to whom the Servant of God successively gave those little booklets to read, written without title, without division of matter, in a hardly legible hand; they bore only the date of the day on which the notes were taken, often also with delay from the day on which the facts narrated had occurred.

p. 906

The reading of those writings edified, and nothing was ever found in them that did not reveal the purely orthodox faith, the profoundly sincere piety, the cruelly severe personal penance of the Servant of God.

Among the persons who frequented the Servant of God and held her as a solid director of souls was the Princess of Fitalia, of Palermo, whom the Servant of God herself esteemed as a beautiful soul. The spiritual intimacy of these two souls brought it about that the Servant of God gave the other some communication of the writings of which we have spoken.

At a certain moment the Princess began to beg and insist with the Servant of God that she consent to those writings being printed.

The resistance and opposition on the part of the Servant of God were great, and she reported it to the undersigned, who, in truth, thinking that one day that material might be spiritual nourishment for many souls, advised the Servant of God to let it be, all the more since the Princess was a very serious person, loved and esteemed by Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Palermo, a Prelate well known as a master of ascetics.

The Princess, having come into possession of the writings with which we are concerned, presented them to His Most Eminent Card. Guarino, who gave of them the judgment that is read in the printed book. Yet, to follow the canonical norms, he handed the writings for review to Canon Pennino of the Chapter of Palermo, himself also a master of ascetics. The opinion of the said reviewer is found in the letter written by him and also reproduced in the book.

It happened, however, that when the printing was done faithfully following the manuscript, and with the approval of the Ecclesiastical Authority, it was seen that that reading produced confusion, and at once the reviewer advised printing the same book, he indicating the title that is read in it and dividing the matter into chapters.

In the book we have is written = Second Edition with additions = Meanwhile everything leads one to believe that the reprint was made only by adding the letter of Can. Pennino and the title indicated by him, because the text is equally printed without divisions into Chapters. This confirms the fact that the Reviewer of the S.C. of Rites, with the manuscript in hand, assures that the book corresponds to it ad litteram: therefore nothing has been removed, added or modified.

Why was this book withdrawn by the Superior Ecclesiastical Authorities?

The undersigned reports what he knows on the matter. At a certain moment a Canonical Visit was ordered for the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. No news was had of any disposition taken by the Visit for the Institute and there resulted from it only the order for the withdrawal of the book in question.

It was not possible to know the reason for this measure, it was only said that that book in the hands of young women could be a cause of ascetic nervous imbalances! and therefore had to be eliminated.

This rumored reason could have its true and prudential side; but why was it handed over to the Holy Office? this can be ascertained only from the same Dicastery, whether the Handing-over was made with motivation. What is certain is that Master Theologians and of Ascetics of the time, and also at present, find nothing in the book either against the Faith or against morals; on the contrary they judge it edifying. As to the opportuneness or not of being able to put it back into circulation, the only judges are the Superior Authorities.

It has been said that at some point of the book an allusion seems to be made to an Ecclesiastical Authority. The undersigned would not know how to find this allusion; only being well aware of something that happened at the time he frequented the Servant of God, he deduces that some allusion could refer to that very fact, which was a true cross for the Servant of God.

The Cardinal Protector of that time, a most worthy person, had an unlimited trust in a very young Sister, who informed in her own way about the affairs of the Institute, not always in conformity with the dispositions of the Servant of God.

The Cardinal, when he frequented the house, went to the study of the Servant of God and there had the other Sister called; on the spot, for the reason indicated above, measures were often taken. For the Servant of God this fact was a true cross and anguish; she would have wished to absent herself, but out of respect for Authority she remained and suffered.

If it is exact that in the book there is some allusion to this suffering, I would not know how to see in it anything of fault.

p. 908

All that is above reported answers, in conscience, to what is known to me regarding the book entitled = Labors and Consolations of the soul on the way of perfection - described by a Servant of God =.

The latter, asked not long ago (as is now customary for all Causes) whether the Cause of Gattorno could be introduced, answered negatively. The reason for this negative answer is the aforesaid book. It will be useful, however, to bear in mind: 1) that others, and not the Servant of God, wanted the printing of those memoirs; 2) that they, before publication, were reviewed and approved by Card. Guarino; 3) that the Censor Theologians found nothing in them against faith and morals; 4) that at present they are entirely out of circulation. To whoever duly considers these circumstances, the negative answer of the Holy Office cannot fail to seem too grave.

IN THE NAME OF THE LORD. AMEN

1. I, the undersigned, by commission regularly entrusted to me, have read, with minute and most lively attention, all the Writings, of a numerous series, of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno; and humbly and tranquilly I set out, in the presence of God, the sentiment I have drawn from them.

2. CURRICULUM VITAE of the Servant of God. Born in Genoa, 14 Oct. 1831: baptized the same day: Parish of Our Lady of the Vines, fortunate for its two sons: Card. Alimonda and Benedict XV. (The Cousin of Benedict XV, Benedetta Carrega, succeeded our Servant of God in the Generalate of the Daughters of St. Anne). - The Family of the Servant of God was distinguished and rich. The parents most pious. - The Servant of God, educated in the Christian manner, grew in piety, in purity, in charity.

At 21, out of obedience to her parents and to her spiritual directors, she accepted marriage with an excellent cousin, Gerolamo Custo. She had three children: Carla, Alessandro, Francesco.

At 27 (in 1857) she was left a widow. Shortly afterward her last child, Francesco, died.

She entrusted the two surviving children, Carlotta and Alessandro, to Christian institutes of education; and she gave herself wholly to works of Holy apostolate.

There was no work of apostolate in Genoa in which the Servant of God did not pour out her whole soul; enjoying the full trust of the Archbishop of well-venerated memory, Andrea Charvaz, and the acquaintance of the admirable Servant of God Giuseppe Frassinetti, brother of Blessed Paola.

At that time she felt drawn to found the Institute, which in fact she instituted. But bound to her still-living parents and to her two surviving children, Carlotta and Alessandro, she turned for light directly to Pius IX; and came to Rome in the first days of January 1866.

Pius IX confirmed and encouraged her in that inspiration. On returning from Rome, Providence disposed that not in Genoa, but in Piacenza, she should open the First House of the Institute, and it was 8 December 1866. In these days the 70 years have been completed.

Difficulties, obstacles in the development of the Institute, are understood. It had its first approval on 31 March 1877; the definitive on 26 July (St. Anne) 1889.

What its progress and its present state, the stones cry out from the wall.

The holy death in Rome: 6 May, Holy Year 1900: of life 69.

3. VIRTUES. The Processes have been made, in which (deducing it from the Writings of the Servant of God, which I have had the grace to go through minutely) the Testimonies must without doubt abound for the happy success of the Cause.

p. 911

Alluding — summarily — to the Virtues, as they burst forth from the Writings, the Servant of God was outstanding and heroic in all the Virtues, to such a degree as to shine among the most extraordinary Saints of the Church.

a) FAITH AND PIETY. My eyes are ever toward the Lord. Her characteristic devotion, of fire, childlike: THE ETERNAL FATHER. Together the Crucifix and the Passion, the Most Holy Eucharist. Mary, St. Joseph, St. Michael, the Guardian Angel, St. Anne, St. Francis of Assisi, her particular exemplar (she was a Tertiary); the Souls in Purgatory. The Church, the Pope. Her piety simple, solid, profound, most tender.

b) HUMILITY. From the Writings it results that, by Grace, she descended, illuminated, as low as the greatest Saints. Meanwhile her exterior did not let transpire (if ever in an infinitesimal part) the great things that God was working in her soul. Manners, ordinary bearing, tranquil, meek, pleasant, gentle, modest, sincere, always smiling; no one could ever have suspected, from her outside, the tremendous Purgatory of love and sorrow that she bore supernaturally, and continually, within herself. — Fruit of Humility, her ardent and industrious gratitude toward Benefactors.

c) LOVE OF GOD. Her union with God, of ever-present awareness and impetus, in the highest modes of mysticism. She is another «Seraphine» like her fellow-citizen St. Catherine of Genoa.

d) LOVE OF NEIGHBOR. From infancy compassion grew with me. One of the greatest «social glories» of the Church in the nineteenth century. Girls, women, the sick. A tender heart, liquefied in charity; attentive and most sensitive and provident to all the smallest things that could help and console the infinite miseries of all. Marvelous, uninterrupted, HEROIC activity, of Catholic action, of good of souls, throughout her life.

e) PRUDENCE. Wisdom, counsel, security of judgment with herself (through the direction and obedience of legitimate Superiors and fathers of spirit), and with others: in forming the government of the Institute she was, in her order, a statesman.

f) FORTITUDE. The valiant woman… in overcoming family affections, of parents and children (whom she loved passionately) in order to be wholly in the things of God. She holily endured the great sorrows caused by her brother Federico (Garibaldian colonel) and by her son Alessandro; sacrificing herself wholly for their spiritual salvation. The great labors and trials inherent in the foundation and propagation of the Institute. Her PENANCES of chains, hair shirts, scourges, fasts, abstinences were, for human nature, simply Frightful, Terrifying; they lasted her whole life, sustained and overcome supernaturally by the sweetness and joy of suffering, according to St. Paul. In this she was like St. Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi and St. Teresa.

g) PRAYER, CONTEMPLATION, continual, elevated, extraordinary, sublime.

4. EXTRAORDINARY GIFTS. They are a great and impressive part of her life. She knew all the temptations, the spiritual desolations: except temptations against chastity. - Visions, apparitions, colloquies, frequent, habitual, so to speak daily, with the Celestials: Our Lord, Our Lady, St. Joseph, St. Michael, the Guardian Angel, St. Anne, St. Francis of Assisi, the Ven. Fr. Bernardo Clausi of the Minims. Stigmata: transverberation of the heart: Crown of thorns: elevations to visions of the Mysteries (Most Holy Trinity, Eucharist, the Holy Child…). Introspection of hearts. Prophecy. Gift of healings. Assaults, infestations of demons. Visions of souls (Prelates, Sisters, and others) who were near to departing this life, or had already passed from it. - Regarding these facts, the Autobiography of the Servant of God will give vast scope to the exercises of students of hysteria, neurasthenia, sentimentalism, etc.; but all the lances will break against the Admirable balance of faculties and of virtues that ALWAYS REIGNED in this great Woman: You have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent, and have revealed them to little ones.

5. MEN OF GOD who had dealings with the Servant of God: Giuseppe Frassinetti, Pius IX, Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro, the Cardinals Alimonda and Verga; and (living) Card. Granito di Belmonte.

6. WRITINGS. They are many. There is a great quantity of Letters (among which, a good number to the prelate Card. Granito di Belmonte). Of supreme importance the personal Memoirs, written out of obedience to the Directors. - IN ALL THE WRITINGS I HAVE NOT NOTED ANYTHING CONTRARY to the Faith or to Morals, nor anything else that, in my view, might stand in the way of the proceeding of the Cause.

There is, however, a delay in this procedure, caused by the publication made in Messina (with the knowledge and praise of the same Card. Archbishop) of a part of the Memoirs of the Servant of God; the part that concerns her Foundations; set out in allegorical form. This Publication passed to the Supreme Congr. of the H.O. In my opinion, I believe I can humbly but firmly assure that in the said Publication (diligently read by me both in the Original and in the Print) there is nothing either against the Faith or against Morals. - Moreover: the Servant of God certainly did not procure the Publication of her Writing; nor, when asked, did she hand it over without warmly recommending that the corrections necessary to the case be made to it. So that, in whatever way it had been published, the Servant of God is free of all guilt and responsibility.

For all these considerations I humbly ask to be permitted to express my most ardent wish, which is that the proceeding of this most noble Cause be delayed no longer. In it, I have the firmest hope, it will shine ever more brightly that the singular ways by which this Foundress was led were illumined by the Spirit of the Lord.

The start of the Cause will bring very great joy to the Genoese, among whom the name and works of Mother Gattorno are held in the highest admiration and religious reverence; to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, by now so glorious; and to the Universal Church, which for 70 years has been nourished also by these heavenly fruits, ripened on the «Rod of Jesse».

Rome, 13 December 1936.

H - TWO STUDIES ON THE SOCIO-RELIGIOUS ENVIRONMENT OF GENOA

AND ON THE SPIRITUAL PHYSIOGNOMY OF ROSA GATTORNO,

FOUNDRESS OF THE CONGREGATION

OF THE DAUGHTERS OF ST. ANNE

1. «The historical environmental humus of Genoa, from the mid-eighteenth century to the birth of Rosa Gattorno», study by Gabriella Airaldi, lecturer in Medieval History at the University of Genoa.

This study by Prof. Gabriella Airaldi brings to light the political, social and religious aspects of the Genoese environment in which the Servant of God was born, was formed and matured her total adherence to the Lord, and it is useful for knowing the premises of her original response to the demands of her time.

The Author, Gabriella Airaldi, is a lecturer in Medieval History at the University of Genoa and Director of the Institute of Medieval Studies of that City.

There are knots, it would perhaps be better to define them as «enigmas» (great and small), in the history of Genoa and of the Genoese that have never been wholly untied. One of the greatest concerns their religiosity and their relationship with the institutions of the Church. The question is not gratuitous and imposes itself in order to try to understand and explain a civilization, an anthropology, such as that of the Genoese, who for nine hundred years made money the base, the pillar and the architrave of their history. By «money» is meant the culture of business in a broad sense, of commerce, of the activity of mediation: a behavior that took off at the dawn of the year One Thousand and, gradually over the centuries, was carried to ever more complex, refined and sophisticated quantitative and qualitative dimensions. The Genoese were masters, at the international level, of administration, investments, credit, discounts, insurance, compound interest: they first created the bases, then realized the most modern forms of capitalism. They were, in substance, great manipulators of capital and bankers. They made money run after the markets, investing almost always in the short term, playing on precise cases, trying to keep fixed their political-geographical positions, almost always strategic: whether they were the trading posts of the East, or the fortunate «bases» in the Iberian Peninsula, in Holland and Flanders, in England.

They were, according to a frequently quoted phrase of the great French historian Fernand Braudel, neo-capitalists ante litteram and, for this reason, in a very broad sense «reformed» two hundred years ahead of the preaching of Luther and Calvin. The objection that arises at this point concerns the geographical position of Genoa, which bordered the lands from which the first «ancestor» movements of Protestantism had moved: Waldensians and Cathars.

A halo, however very vague, of «heresy» brushed Genoa in the Middle Ages: on the other hand, in the seafaring Commune, there were never, beside fierce and bloody political feuds between the major families, wars of religion. The Genoese, although precise documents on the matter are lacking, seem for the most part detached from the problems of religion and theology, as well as from disputes about orthodoxy. They were largely tolerant toward the Jews (few in number, however, in Genoa, also because the Genoese carried on competing activities) and even toward the Muslims (with whom they had commercial contacts in the medieval age) and to whom they granted, during captivity awaiting ransom, a mild and tolerated practice of their religion.

Of the Genoese, especially of the ruling classes, we know some aspects, also of private life: austere customs, scant inclination to frivolities, to amusements, to festivities. In Genoa the fashion of Carnival did not take hold, even in the Modern age, and the activity of theater and spectacle had neither great expansion nor diffusion.

The government of public affairs always had a precise «lay» connotation, with a precise separation (perhaps also because of the prevailing economic and business activity, always at risk of ecclesiastical condemnation for «usury» in the Middle Ages, according to a well-known definition of St. Thomas Aquinas) between political choices and the spiritual-ecclesial sphere. Yet one never hears of lack of respect toward the Bishop: on the contrary, the institutions always showed themselves formally respectful. The younger sons of the great families of noble-merchants were almost always members of the Chapter of Canons and often ascended to the episcopal see. In the thirteenth century there were two Genoese popes; from the mid-fifteenth century to the first decade of the sixteenth some four Ligurian popes are counted. In the cardinalatial Sacred College the Ligurians were always three or four (out of about thirty Cardinals, on average).

One therefore has the clear sensation of a society substantially conservative in custom (and therefore austere in behavior and rigid and severe in the sphere of judgments on private life), little inclined to speculations of pure theology, which distributed and weighed public roles. The Bishop therefore had his part, but though an important and delicate part, it was never a hegemonic part. Paolo di Campofregoso, cardinal, who was, in the thirty-eight years in which he held the office of Archbishop of Genoa (in the second half of the fifteenth century), at times Doge, remains a singular exception.

But there is more. Since the golden years of Genoese expansion in the East, in the thirteenth century, the merchant-bankers lent themselves to supporting «missionary churches», parishes, prelatures nullius and bishoprics in what could justly be defined as «mission land»: it must not be forgotten that until the sixteenth century people still spoke of «Crusade». The Genoese, obviously, did not distinguish themselves by missionary spirit: they tolerated respectfully, they cultivated the institutional alliance with the Church, from which they undoubtedly derived advantages of a political and diplomatic order. It matters little if of many parishes and bishoprics only the nominal investiture remained, to religious of large families who never saw the shores of Syria, of Constantinople or of the ports of the Black Sea.

p. 920

There remains, even in these «colonial» behaviors, the constant of a correct and respectful alliance: nor can one pass over in silence the relevance — this indeed wholly emotional and of custom — of a widespread religiosity, perhaps not devoid of superstition and even of residues of paganism, in a people accustomed to going to sea, with all the risks that such a life entailed. Proof of it are the churches, the rural parishes built almost everywhere along the coasts, the chapels perched sheer over the sea and the ex-votos.

As regards, still and more deeply, life within the city-state of Genoa, the role of private charity must be underlined. Considering that the State had scant margins of intervention, economic and military life being dominated by the autonomous initiative of the great families, the sphere of the «social» was annexed to private persons. And so it falls to private persons, who intervene moved not only by political-social motives and of public order, but also and above all by a very strong sense of solidarity which perhaps sinks genetically into the roots of a people that has always lived surrounded by difficulties of communication and grappling with that «enemy» (which is nonetheless the source of all sustenance and also of wealth and well-being) which is the sea.

In this type of intervention women stand beside men. In Genoa, the role of woman is singular and shows differences, in comparison with other peoples and other States, since the Middle Ages: the woman, because of the absence of the man (father, husband, brother, sons, relative), far away, at sea, must of necessity face important problems of daily life. And it is not only a matter of the education and care of the children, but of the need to intervene on the patrimony: dowries, wills, purchases and sales, mortgages: these are realities that require a precise culture and a non-subordinate knowledge of the affairs of the house.

We have, therefore, women who exercise, albeit in the «private» sphere, dominant roles and functions, which then give, within the house and the family, a different position. Yet to women, in Genoa, political power is not granted, nor are they directed to higher studies. They intervene when necessary, in the absence of men, but immediately withdraw into the shadows. The phenomenon of the monastic option is, however, fairly widespread, both in the great families and at middle and lower levels.

p. 921

But it is not necessarily from the religious orders that the most conspicuous social and welfare interventions descend. There is — and this element remains a precise constant — a constant mobilization of volunteering, also within the great families. Genoese gentlewomen unite — while remaining wives and mothers — to intervene on behalf of those who suffer: generally the victims of epidemics, of famines, of poverty and of chronic illness.

The example of Caterina Fieschi Adorno (1447-1510), popularly known as St. Catherine of Genoa, belonging to one of the two or three greatest families of the city, is emblematic. Before undertaking her mission within the Hospital of Pammatone, founded in the first half of the fifteenth century by a very rich jurist, Bartolomeo Bosco, and of which she would become for a decade «Rectress», she will find her luminous charitable path through volunteering, drawn in by other ladies, older than she, devoted to the relief of the dispossessed and of the sick.

The charitable and hospital vein will in any case, as will be seen later, be a precise leitmotiv of the «social» history of Genoa, with a constant presence of women (especially of high family extraction), always accompanied by support for/from the Church. And this continuity of intervention and presence will have the discreet but considerable material, that is, economic, support of the ruling classes.

One can therefore untangle the threads, rather snarled, regarding the initial question on religiosity in Genoa, identifying some tendencies, all juxtaposed. There exists a constant religiosity and devotion of women, who assume, in the context of social dynamics, the function of executive arm of charitable and welfare intervention, often of vast scope and therefore substituting for the «public» role; there exists a charismatic presence of the Bishop and of the Curial Hierarchy, strong but never predominant, also because the phenomenon of interaction between the great families and the Church remains relevant, to which they willingly lend their younger sons and their daughters not destined for marriage; there exists, at the same time, a sort of «secularity» steeped in tolerance, as regards a great part of the management of business and of state-family politics. The less confessional component of the culture of the Genoese ruling classes does not, however, aim at a conflict of ideological type or even merely of power with the ecclesiastical sphere, but limits itself to acting in watertight compartments, though in formal respect of the hierarchy and of all the outward manifestations of religiosity: the most conspicuous example of this conception and of this way of acting remains Andrea Doria, on the threshold of the Modern Age, who considers the Papacy and the episcopate of the city as political interlocutors, with whom balances, relations of force, alliances and also retaliations are to be built, when political urgency and the general interest require it.

Even though there is no material and documentary proof, one may venture, with a wide margin of approximation, that indifference, steeped in pragmatic spirit, and fervent religious commitment, reflected however always in action (St. Catherine of Genoa is the example of a mystic who travels her purest contemplative and speculative «iter» through a very concrete action of solidarity) are two constants, not opposed, but co-present in the humus and in the roots of the culture and in the system of values of Genoa from the Crusades to the modern age. Down to the last decades of the existence of the Republic (of which the Virgin had been proclaimed Queen, to avert coups d'état, in the second half of the seventeenth century), from when the investigation that now interests us takes its start.

Genoese society presents characteristics of «originality», therefore, throughout the Middle Ages and the whole Modern Age: maintaining, as an oligarchy (above all in the city, but not always over the whole regional territory), full political autonomy and independence alongside a system that continues to produce great wealth and capital, remains a peculiarity, a characterization also sociological that stands apart from the normality of other Italian and even European situations (leaving aside the dimension and function of the great powers of the continent from the end of the fifteenth century onward).

In Genoa capitalist accumulation, managed with modernity of systems, projects, also in the collective imagination, the socio-cultural myth of an «individual» perfectly free (unbound) to act in an economic system of great elasticity.

At the same time, the «private» (privatistic) management of public affairs — one need only think of the interweaving of interests and interactions between the Signoria (with its institutions: the Dogeship, the two Councils, etc.) and the Bank of St. George — in the hands of a business oligarchy prevents a real sense of the State from forming, even in consciences.

It is precisely its natural dimension as a port city of very great international importance that leads the Genoese to model singular schemes of «acceptance-rejection» which often disregard ideological demands. Being a coagulation of capital, in the heart of a poor agricultural area of very scarce territorial resources, provokes, on the contrary, continual phenomena of urbanization: a physiognomy which, macroscopic in the capital, is in any case repeated, as an organizational and even residential-building scheme, over the whole Ligurian territory. In any case, the hypertrophy of urbanization avoids implosion, because, in the colonial medieval age, it gives rise to compensating and rebalancing migratory hemorrhages. This behavior too ends by becoming physiological and leads, in the modern age as well and in subsequent epochs, to new situations of obligatory emigration.

In this key, it is worth underlining the role, this too wholly singular, of a Church that thus lives a centrifugal and missionary function, tied to the diaspora of business and which, at the same time, must always perform a mediating and moderating function between the embittered political factions intra moenia.

To these considerations of a general character, other serious motives for reflection must be added, as one approaches the epoch one wishes to consider. In the first place, a sort of «reductio ad unum» of the history of Genoa is not easy (already for the Middle Ages, but even more so as regards the Modern Age): dispersion outside the civic and Ligurian context interrupts flows and concentrations of a political character and of lines of tendency, fragmenting not only the choices but even the facts, the events in themselves. In the Middle Ages, in any case, when Genoa performs the function of a thalassocratic power that can, if not equal, at least stand beside — on the military and diplomatic plane — the greater kingdoms of the continent and the very interlocutors of the East, it is still possible to discern and untangle some threads that can be catalogued as leitmotiv.

For the Modern Age it is more difficult, not to say arduous, because Genoese history, passing through vicissitudes limiting terms of habitual behavior, with decades of authentic défaillance, is outlined as an apparently «reduced» development, also in terms of narrative: it is a somewhat heterogeneous summation of events and behaviors, encompassed and decidedly «in tow» of far greater events of more pregnant import.

Put in plain words: after the death of Andrea Doria, who exploits Genoa's financial and military-maritime potential in the function of a «partnership» in an inferior position, though always honorable and remunerative for its class of noble-businessmen, with regard to the Spain of Charles V, of Philip II and of their successors, Genoa slides toward a clear political decline. Little by little, the war fleet too loses its importance and shrinks in size almost to disappearing. The port, on the commercial plane, is saved because, at the end of the sixteenth century and throughout the seventeenth and beyond, it remains flourishing and active as a «free port», to allow the advantageous monopoly of the grain trade. International finance, even with ruinous losses, when the Spanish Crown cancels the debts contracted with the Genoese bankers, still holds and tends to shift toward new markets: Flanders (already frequented), Holland and England.

The ruling class of noble bankers and brokers — here too against the current — finds its period of outward opulence, that is, building fabulous residences, furnished by great artists with splendor and display of power, precisely in the midst of the Counter-Reformation. But here too one must underline the tendency to austerity of life, to outward rigor and in any case to a solid luxury, where there are no concessions to that phenomenon which today is defined, perhaps a little superficially, as the «ephemeral».

The economic class, in short, continues to play a leading role internationally, becoming mediator of flows of money from the New World to Europe and in circulation within Europe itself. Genoa, unlike Venice, can do without transforming itself into a land Duchy, like the Triveneto, after the advent of the Ottoman Empire and the loss of territorial possessions in the East: it remains a «business committee» which, however, on the political and diplomatic plane, having neither territory nor natural resources to maintain a minimum of army, cannot compete at the international level. Genoa will pass, after the naval bombardment ordered by Louis XIV in 1684, from the orbit of Spain to that of France, on the plane of foreign-policy alliances and so will curl up like a hedgehog, an earthen pot among iron pots throughout the seventeenth century. The episodes of which the weary Maritime Republic is protagonist are emblematic: from the «question of the Finale» to the episode, later become oleographic and of popular legend, of the riots called of Balilla (1747), in which Genoa maneuvers among the appetites of its neighbors — France, Austria and Piedmont — until the cession of Corsica to France (1768) because of the impossibility of quelling the autonomist movements.

Napoleon Bonaparte, liquidating the aristocratic Republic in 1797, will bury, politically speaking, a corpse.

Genoa, therefore, which from the mid-sixteenth century to the end of the eighteenth loses ever more its political weight in Italy and in Europe, now presents itself as a small, thinly populated state with very scarce natural resources. Yet, as already hinted, if the decline is objective, the aristocratic ruling class has maintained its ancient peculiarity: it remains very rich, with its capital placed in all Countries and with investments of the capital itself that yield very high interest.

In the last decades of the eighteenth century, Genoa begins to pay for the endemic fragility of its internal political system, based on power held by a few dozen families which, in practice, in the complex interplay of interconnection between the State and the Bank of St. George, control all the offices and also the system of access to them. The oligarchic system was fairly closed already in the Middle Ages: yet, at the moment of the institution of the first Dogeship (the perpetual one), there had been the insertion of the «new nobles» alongside and, in part, in place of the «old nobles». The successive constitutions, from that of Andrea Doria (1528) to the so-called «of Casale» (1576), made the system ever more rigid and closed, precluding all turnover.

Power is exclusively in the hands of the aristocracy, at whose summit is the Doge (biennial from 1528), flanked by the «Most Serene Colleges». This aristocracy is interested in maintaining the «status quo», even though through its philanthropic paternalism (hospitals, dowries for poor girls, payments for the redemption of popular taxes) it earns the devotion of the common people and of the countryside: there is a custom, of charitable inspiration, even of distributing grain and foodstuffs to the inhabitants of the mountains, when they came down to Genoa in winter, because of the frequent famines. For this purpose a precise public function was instituted: the Magistracy of Abundance.

In the second half of the eighteenth century a decidedly lively and enterprising «middle» bourgeoisie takes shape.

It is a middle bourgeoisie which, not being noble, is excluded, by virtue of the «Constitution of Casale», from public offices and from political and administrative responsibilities, but which, in fact, is acquiring ever greater spaces and weight in a society ever more complex and articulated. The phenomenon, in truth, is the same as was being observed throughout the European West and which has its peak in the cities. In England, a century earlier, this middle bourgeoisie, united with the lower and middle clergy of the Anglican church, pragmatically achieved its political aims with the celebrated «revolution of the brewers» of Oliver Cromwell. In France, the richest, most cultured and most evolved Country of Europe, with the diffusion of Enlightenment ideas, those ferments were stirring that would later have provoked the Revolution. In Italy, fragmented into so many small States, where a Catholic-moderate and paternalistic interpretation of the Enlightenment dominated throughout the central-northern area, because of the policy of reforms of Maria Theresa and of Joseph II of Austria, and where a determining role is exercised by the presence of the Papal State, it is difficult to find, at a statistically relevant level, a political and socio-economic movement tied to a bourgeoisie in motion. But Genoa, as has already been observed, has wholly particular characteristics. In the first place, it is a city where since the Middle Ages there has existed a very strong, indeed exclusive, urban culture. Moreover, its aristocracy and even its clergy are informed by values and behaviors of a bourgeois-mercantile stamp. Between the institutional ruling class and the growing middle class there is a specular interplay. Thus a stratum is slowly being created, formed of «liberal» nobles, small bankers, merchants, wholesalers, port operators, small shipowners, notaries, lawyers, physicians, artisans of sturdy dimensions (almost «industrialists»): a «middle class», decidedly well-off, passably (or even very) educated, which receives French books and is not insensible to Jacobin propaganda. At the same time, in the religious sphere, men, but above all women, are sensitive to the diffusion of Jansenist ideas. This too, on the religious and moral plane, is a phenomenon that presents a historical continuity. It has been said that Genoa, while mostly rejecting theological disputes and religious polemics, is pervaded by a certain «reformed» spirit. Jansenism, with its rigorism, with the perspective of placing man's conscience at the center of ethical elaboration, comes close to the rigors of Calvinism. It makes man responsible, but at the same time makes him freer and more autonomous in his choices: hence, as is then evident from the beginning of the ideal phenomena that led to the Italian Risorgimento, of which Genoa is certainly the cradle, the rapprochement between the ideals (albeit laicist) of the Risorgimento and of Liberalism and the religiosity of Jansenist structure. Father Eustachio Degola, confessor and counselor of Maria Drago, the mother of Giuseppe Mazzini, is in the odor of Jansenism. And precisely the «Apostle of the Unity of Italy», albeit outside the Church, appears as the syncretic product of that culture and of that society.

This explains, beyond the opportunisms, great and small, which in great events of this kind always occur, the genuine enthusiasm provoked, in 1797, by the fall of the Aristocratic Republic, in the prospect of giving life to a democratic republic, of a vaguely Jacobin stamp. It must not be forgotten that, beyond the caste privilege that the aristocracy was losing, the French Revolution brings with it the gospel and the consequent political application of economic liberalism, a creed that in Genoa adapts very well to the cultural anthropology of the city, considering that the ruling class for centuries and centuries had moved with the greatest ease and unscrupulousness. France, in this sense, in the few years in which the Democratic Republic holds (albeit surreptitiously, because without French arms it would not have survived alone), aims to make of Genoa a true anti-Austrian and anti-Piedmontese bulwark. The whirlwind events of 1796-97 confirm it: the «democratic» Genoese bourgeoisie is beside the French against the English (great rivals on the seas), Austrians and Piedmontese (the potential «invaders» by land). And the commercial and business city is wholly for Napoleon, while the conservative pockets are strong in the more agrarian valleys, sensitive to the old paternalism, Valpolcevera and Valbisagno. This will lead to a widening of participation in public affairs and to the suppression of the religious orders, the Jesuits in the first place, even though the historic merit of having really created and shaped the University of Genoa belongs to the Society of Jesus: but the Jesuits in Genoa, though then performing throughout the following century a preeminent role in the education of the city's ruling class, must also suffer sharp peaks of unpopularity. In Genoa, precisely in that wake where the perfume of Port Royal still breathes, the protagonists, in close relation with the ruling class which they form in their schools, in parishes and in private teaching, are the Barnabites, substantially tied to a certain sympathy for liberal Catholicism. It is perhaps right to underline, in order to identify the great strands of behavior and of «systems of values» that circulate not only among the summits of the ruling and aristocratic class, but also among the emerging middle bourgeoisie, entrepreneurial, professional and commercial, at least three paths: the first, tied to the Jesuits and to the traditional Church; the second, connected to liberal Catholicism, of Jansenist inspiration, which seeks to reconcile faith and unitary and Risorgimento ideals; the third, of Jacobin descent, decidedly lay and Enlightenment-positivist. From this last trunk, not without indirect influences from the second, will come the Mazzinian, Garibaldian and democratic movements.

The ruling class — enlarged to that «second band» of economic and cultural-professional operators which the wind of the French Revolution thickens, giving it a precise economic-social role of Genoa (but also its customs, its mentality, its system of values) — is formed in a modern key precisely in the years in which the fragile «Democratic Republic» is transformed into a province of the Empire of Napoleon. In precisely this epoch the link (made closer by pre-industrial evolution) between Genoa and Milan, capital of the Cisalpine Republic, is born. In Genoa the loss of political autonomy is lamented only in part, because, thanks precisely to the privileged channel of economic relations with Lombardy, the entrepreneurial ruling class finds interesting outlets and a market, inbound and outbound thanks to the port, of ever vaster horizons. Yet, in that period, the «provisional government» made up of nobles (but not in the majority), of landowners and of professionals, discusses and deliberates on «revolutionary» subjects, such as: public works in function of the social and moral growth of the people, civil and political rights, the role of women. Into this dialogue, indeed into the debate, the Archbishops often insert themselves, as a complementary, balancing element, in the wake of a precise tradition going back eight hundred years. But the turbulent period of the Napoleonic wars does not allow great socio-economic growth. Not only that: the Congress of Vienna, as is known, decides that the territories of the former Republic of Genoa be annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia. The Genoese of the ruling class desperately try to avoid the union. They offer the whole territory of Liguria to Talleyrand and Metternich, but ask that Genoa (and a minimum of hinterland) remain a free zone and above all a free port, on condition, obviously, of denying equal privilege to all the ports of the arc of the Ligurian Sea (up to and beyond Nice) and of the northern Tyrrhenian (Livorno). The Genoese economic class therefore does not speak in the name of the people, of liberty and of patriotism, but is driven by a precise selfish calculation (which will be spent, years later, as a resurgence of defense of national identity).

On the other hand, in 1815, the situation is not rosy: in Genoa heavy taxes are feared to maintain the Savoy Court and the large army; the system is contested, dear to the old Sardinian state, bureaucratic, agrarian and retrograde, based on territorial levies and customs duties. In the port coastal trade is in decline, there are only two ships covering the Atlantic routes, the grain market is controlled, and even contacts have been lost with the tuna-fisheries and with the first rudimentary canning industries which had precisely in Liguria their epicenter.

Genoa, in practice, from 1815 to 1840 undergoes a sort of military protectorate. The city (which does not yet have the coastal municipalities and those of the valleys annexed and is limited to the present historic center or little more) numbered about 80 thousand inhabitants. Yet it is watched over by 8,600 garrison soldiers and defended by an iron curtain of forts and casemates, restructured, strengthened and completed. Already from 1821 dissensions begin: those three ideal and political-religious «strands» are outlined with violence, to the point that King Charles Felix closes the University from 1821 to 1823. Genoa appears at this point as a contradictory reality: it suffers the damages of the traditionalist and paleo-economic policy of Piedmont, whence vast pockets of misery are determined, accompanied by marginalization, both in the city, where those employed in industry are still 10% of the active population, and in the Rivieras and in the hinterland, where the division of property and the endemic lack of resources force many populations to emigrate. Productive activities are still primitive: milling, olive-oil, extractive industry, or paper mills, soap works and, only partially, textiles, thanks to the widespread custom of divisions of labor, fragmented in the homes and entrusted above all to women. Shipbuilding holds, but still only in the Rivieras.

Yet many social diseases and epidemics are widespread, which wreak havoc in an undernourished and wasted population: petechial typhus, cholera, contagious dysentery, besides lung-type affections. Infant mortality exceeds 40 per thousand.

Only slowly do general conditions improve: a part of the customs duties begins to be eliminated, roads and communications are improved, old and important business relations are resumed, also on foreign markets (from Portugal to Spain, from England to Holland). The shipping companies and shipowners (among whom the star of Raffaele Rubattino emerges) understand the importance of steam and begin to abandon sailing brigantines.

At the end of the Twenties of the last century, the situation evolves: local journalism distinguishes itself by a high-level debate between liberals and democratic Catholics, while the conditions for an economic recovery mature.

Genoa becomes, little by little, an economic «laboratory», but also a political-social one. This, above all from the mid-Thirties, up to the First War of Independence. It is Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, who treasures the Genoese experience lived by him, barely twenty, as an officer of the Engineers. Cavour observes that the ruling, financial and entrepreneurial class of the city has a potential of expansion far superior to the slight dimensions of the Kingdom of Sardinia. It can be the economic class of the united Italy of tomorrow. Not only that: if the natural and «physiological» inclinations of this economic class are seconded, the attitude of hostility of the Genoese toward Piedmont and its policy of expansion will cease.

Cavour exploits the first timid industrial presences along the coasts of the centers of the Genoese Ponente (Sampierdarena, Cornigliano, Sestri) and transforms those first industries of partly foreign capital (such as Taylor and Prandi, ancestor of Ansaldo) into great centers for mechanics, steelmaking and shipbuilding. It will thus be that the ruling class and the middle-bourgeois one will abandon the post-Napoleonic dream of the republic, of autonomy and, in part, of Mazzinianism, to embrace the moderate liberalism dear to Cavour. There thus arises an unwritten pact between the economic world and the architect of the unity of Italy. This explains the recovery of Garibaldi and the not marginal role of Raffaele Rubattino.

The religious world too, and the more specific one of the official Church, present articulated situations. In the first place, it must be noted that the charitable, philanthropic and welfare tendency does not cease, indeed it is channeled along the tradition already marked by St. Catherine Fieschi Adorno or by Blessed Virginia Centurione Bracelli.

At the beginning of the century, Genoa knows the great charity of the Holy Father, so acclaimed still in life (St. Francesco da Camporosso). At the head of the Church, throughout the century, archbishops of varied tendency and also of different weight succeed one another: from the great and moderate Lambruschini, future Secretary of State of the Vatican, to Tardini, to whom is owed, in the Thirties, the reopening of the Diocesan Synod. Yet political difficulties lead to a full six years of vacant episcopal see, until the appointment of Archbishop Charvaz, held to be pro-Savoy, but who managed to handle a long period of peaceful coexistence with political power. Then it is the turn of Archbishop Magnasco, a man of great charity but judged an intransigent conservative.

During these administrations, the needs of social intervention of the less well-off and less assisted population mature. It must not be forgotten that if Giuseppe Mazzini will found the first workers' association in 1851, already in 1854 we have the first Catholic workers' society, while from the second half of the century, to underline a phenomenon too conspicuous not to be tied to a precise historical need, numerous women's congregations are founded.

In the same years an important Salesian house will be founded by Don John Bosco, and the Catholic political daily «Il Cittadino».

In this so difficult period, almost of «permanent revolution», which forms the background to the youth and formation of Rosa Gattorno, the meeting point and the overcoming of clashes remains the early and concrete implementation of a mature and conscious solidarism, lived in the new society and in the values it goes on proposing. A social instance that functions as a meeting point of opposite extremisms. Indeed, between the pushes toward a new industrialization and the struggles between conservatives and innovators, it is the lower social strata that pay the price. Genoa already exceeds 100 thousand inhabitants: but 50 thousand cannot read. Between the rich and the middle class only twenty thousand pay taxes: the other eighty thousand are exempt for insufficient income. Even the land register is imprecise and civil registry is lacking.

Heart of advanced political experiences, Genoa shows that the course of things cannot be stopped. Besides, at the end of the century the «Rerum Novarum» of Leo XIII is the living demonstration of how much road — beyond the painful «Roman question» — the Church traveled in the same period.

Intensely lived, even in the most distant past, as a corrective to the material vision of life, the social instance, which goes on assuming more complete and definitive contours, represents the true and definitive epochal revolution: the religious world lives it and modifies it.

Rosa Gattorno is not an isolated case, a rhapsodic exception, but corresponds to the history and anthropology of Genoa and of Liguria. She is further testimony of a holiness with contours of perfectibility, reached through the balance between action and purifying and cathartic mystical aspiration, which has its roots well planted in the tormented Genoese history.

It is difficult to assemble a comprehensive bibliography on the period that is the object of the present study. There exist, in fact, no works of synthesis; and, when they exist, they treat very specific themes, often neglecting the interrelations, which must therefore be reconstructed at every turn. The material for consultation is found for the most part scattered in local reviews (such as the Rassegna storica della Liguria or the Bollettino Linguistico, or the Atti della Società Ligure di Storia Patria) or national ones, besides in the «classic» histories of Genoa, which, however, for the most part stop at the pre-Risorgimento age.

INTRODUCTION

Complying with the wish of Mother A. Virginia Sinagra, superior general of the Daughters of St. Anne, I accepted the welcome task of studying the personality of Mother Rosa Gattorno, one of the most successful foundresses among the many the Church had in the second half of the nineteenth century. But I must confess that, finding myself before the mass of the writings of the Servant of God, the problems raised around her Cause of Canonization and the complexity of the manifestations of her spirituality, in certain respects truly disconcerting, I remained somewhat perplexed.

As I went further into the analytical reading of the rich testimony of herself left in her Memoirs and in her book Labors and Consolations, however, I saw her spiritual and apostolic figure grow larger. This image was then offered to me in all its evangelical dimension in comparing the results of my study with the hundreds of cards drawn from the letters of the Foundress […].

If we had only as a source of information the external testimony of the depositions of the witnesses who were heard in the various ordinary processes, everything would have been easy; in fact, the fortunate foundress, as her contemporaries saw her, especially her spiritual daughters and the various personalities who dealt with her intimately, appears as a soul of high union with God, of intrepid faith, full of charity and sacrifice, of goodness, of humility, most penitent, adorned with charismatic gifts of every sort. But it was precisely the image of herself traced by her in her writings, concretely in the book Labors and Consolations, that gave rise to the Dilata of the Holy Office, when in 1932 the Congregation of Rites asked for the nihil obstat for the introduction of the Cause. In 1979 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (former Holy Office) granted the nihil obstat, asking, however, that «the state of normality or not» of the Servant of God be studied. Then the Congregation for the Causes of Saints judged a medical-psychic expert opinion necessary.

Fr. Paolino Zavarella, doctor in Medicine, with his most weighty and exhaustive «votum», came to dispel definitively every shadow of uncertainty: Rosa Gattorno was a woman not only fully normal from the psychic point of view, but endowed with a notable intellectual and volitional balance, as well as extraordinary practical sense, enterprising initiative and easy human relations; qualities which, elevated and enriched by supernatural gifts, won her the esteem and veneration of relevant civil and ecclesiastical personalities! […].

I. THE HUMAN RECEPTACLE OF GOD'S ACTION

[…]

1. The family and social environment

Rosa was born on 14 October 1831 in the bosom of a Genoese family of good social position and profound Christian sentiments. She was the second of six siblings, three boys and three girls, to whom must be added the half-sister, whom the mother had in her first marriage. Her father, Francesco Gattorno, was devoted to commercial affairs. It seems that he had a very positive influence on the human formation of his daughter, first of all in the sense that the filial relationship with him predisposed her to a special relationship with God the Father; in one of her writings Mother Rosa mentions the security that is drawn from paternal affection «which can never deceive». We may also attribute to paternal influence that administrative capacity which she would later show. From the father's correspondence there results a relationship of great trust and affectionateness.

As regards religious and moral orientation Rosa was indebted, from infancy, to the solicitous care of her mother, Adelaide Campanella, a woman of notable piety and sensitive character. The mutual understanding between mother and daughter was total.

Rosa lived at close hand the political and ideological turmoil that agitated Italian society, concretely the Genoese, in the years of her infancy and youth. A maternal uncle of hers, Federico Campanella, was part of the Ligurian committee of Young Italy. In 1883 he had to take refuge in the Gattorno house to escape capture; exiled in France, he returned in 1848; he succeeded in drawing to his Masonic and
