It was a hard blow for our young woman; it helped her to strengthen her adherence to the Church and to the Pope. Federico's clearly anti-religious position will be for her whole life a thorn in her heart, as appears in a letter of 13 May 1897 to Princess Emilia di Fitalia. He, however, despite his ideological positions, nourished a true veneration for his sister, held by him to be a «saint»; so he will proclaim her in 1907 in open parliament (FIOCCHI, I, p. 2). Both he and his brother Francesco, who testified in the informative process of Genoa, kept the memory of Rosa as that of an angel of peace and goodness in the midst of the family (cf. Summ., p. 648-649).

At the age of 21 Rosa contracted marriage, more by the will of her parents than by her own inclination, according to many of the testimonies, with Gerolamo Custo, himself also a merchant of international scope. The life of wife and mother would become for her a source of great sacrifices and a school of heroic virtues. The first trial was the economic bankruptcy of her husband in his business in Marseille; reduced to poverty, they were received in the house of Rosa's father. Second trial: the firstborn Carlotta, because of an illness that struck at a tender age, became deaf-mute. Three years later Alessandro was born. The husband, in 1857, left for Russia on a commercial venture that went well for him; but he had to return sick with tuberculosis. In December of that year the third child, Francesco, was born. A faithful and loving wife, Rosa stayed in those months beside the bed of her husband, who was slowly dying, until he died on 9 March 1858. Besides conjugal affection, there was between the two also a consonance of spirits: during the illness they held spiritual conversations between themselves, as they were accustomed to do before, when Gerolamo was in health.

To the grief of the loss of her husband and of the orphanhood of her three children there came to be added, already at the funeral, the quarrel between the two families. Rosa saw all her goods seized, even the furniture of her house; and again she was received with her children in her father's house. Three months later the youngest, Francesco, died, leaving her inconsolable.

Her own sorrow and her own privations helped her to open her heart to the sufferings and needs of others, and to discover the meaning of suffering in the embrace of her Crucified.

2. Culture and intellectual gifts

Families of the social level of the Gattorno sent, in that epoch, their sons to public schools, while for the instruction of the daughters provision was made by calling into the house teachers of Italian letters, of French, of drawing and of music. Rosa succeeded in acquiring particular skill in embroidery, as also in singing and the piano; she was invited to sing and play at family feasts (FIOCCHI, I, p. 7, 17). She had to perfect the rudiments of the French language in the brief stay with her husband in Marseille; later the practice of this language would be useful to her in her journeys to France as foundress (M 9.5, p. 1-30).

Judging from the writings, it cannot be said that the literary culture of Rosa Gattorno surpassed the average level: she writes with many spelling mistakes, neglects punctuation, uses frequent dialect expressions and endings. But she possesses a surprising ease in composition, which allows her to write for many hours a day without interruption. She also has the gift of varying the type of composition according to the content and purpose of what she writes. In her Letters she adopts a lively, incisive, vigorous language, full of sincerity and immediacy, not free of a certain causticity, always however cordial and affectionate, and different according to the addressee. In the Memoirs, written out of an inner need to give expression to what she experiences and lives secretly, without having in mind any other addressee than her supreme Good, feelings count more than ideas; she puts down quickly in writing what at the moment she feels or remembers, interjects exclamations, does not care for the structure of the sentence. On the other hand, in her book Labors and Consolations, which she knew would be printed and circulated, her privileged intelligence suggested to her, for understandable reasons, a wholly different style: a succession of allegorical pictures, ingenious and fully original, with a surprising variety of images and richness of lexicon; it is difficult to identify the author of the book with that of the Memoirs.

But it is precisely this unique facility for allegorizing that offers us the key to interpret what, as we shall see, is a constant of her intimate experience: the uninterrupted sequence of her visions and demonic representations. The culture of Rosa Gattorno is typically a culture of the symbol, to which the language of mystics in general refers, by virtue of the need they have to overcome the limit of human expression by symbolizing the concepts, experienced more than mentally elaborated.

As regards the religious culture of the Servant of God, one certainly cannot speak of a theological formation that exceeds that received in catechesis and through preaching and reading. In her writings we find frequent quotations from sacred Scripture, made from memory in a form often imprecise; sometimes she puts under the phrase «says the holy Gospel» texts of the Psalms or of St. Paul. She likes to cite examples from the lives of the Saints; in a conference to the sisters she explained this hagiographical erudition of hers: «These things I know for having read them in books, and not by any other way».

The two censors of the writings pointed out certain terminological inexactitudes, as when, several times, she uses the expression apostatic union — in place of hypostatic — to indicate the experience of a very high union with God, a sense very different from that which it has in theology (cf. M 1.2, p. 122f; 12.1, p. 26).

3. Character and temperament

The data on which we must trace the characterological features of Mother Rosa, both the autobiographical ones and those gathered from testimonies, belong for the most part to the stage of her life as a consecrated woman; therefore it is not easy to distinguish what reveals a natural way of being of hers from what, instead, is the fruit of an itinerary of purification and of overcoming her own defects, of progress in the virtues. In any case it is always a matter of components of her personality, placed at the service of that great love which is the motive of her whole existence.

A strong and courageous spirit

A woman of character is how those who knew her define her. The Benedictine Don Domenico Serafini, who had been for two years, during Mother Rosa's life, apostolic visitor of the Daughters of St. Anne, describes her as «a woman of piety, of an extraordinary mind and of much energy».

In the critical moments of her life she showed herself mistress of herself, resolute and courageous. Thus, for example, in family events, as wife and as widow; in the alternative of leaving her own children and parents to consecrate herself to the interests of God; in the attitude taken toward persons and situations, some strong and humiliating, which she had to face as foundress.

Ill from the beginning of her widowhood, weakened by fasts, vigils and other penances, subject moreover to the pain of the hidden stigmata and to the burnings of the heart, which produced frequent fainting in her, she worked tirelessly in her office, undertook long and heavy journeys, visited the houses of the Institute listening to all the sisters, dealt with prelates and benefactors…; and she managed to master her own weakness and fatigue, so as to appear, as the saying goes, always in form […].

In the catalog of the virtues there is one that is linked to fortitude, virtue and gift of the Holy Spirit, and receives the name of magnanimity and also of audacity: it helps to overcome pusillanimity before obstacles to be surmounted. In a note to Mons. Granito di Belmonte Mother Rosa wrote:

«A line in haste, to give you good news: I have made the contract for the schools (in Naples), and they are already at work. Long live audacity! What do you say? It is not audacity, but only confidence in my God» (L 22-9-1896).

Here is the secret of that energy of character which caused admiration: Mother Rosa was a woman of faith; she was sure that, in her own weaknesses, she could always count on the fortitude of God: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13). And she was convinced of having God on her side, since the Institute founded by her was the Work of the Lord; hence in her writings the well-known text of St. Paul leaps out now and then: If God is for us, who will be against us? (Rom 8:31).

7 Deposition at the Roman Process, Sess. CIII. Serenity and balance

Weighed in her words, affable and sweet with all, letting the unalterable peace of her spirit show through in her gaze: so her contemporaries saw her according to the testimonies of the informative processes. The Princess of Fitalia, when she was presented to Gattorno for the first time, had «a great impression of imposingness, like a queen of extraordinary austerity and of great sweetness together» (Summ., p. 427).

But what no one guessed was the price of such a

conquest in a strong and passionate temperament like hers. Here is how she saw herself in February 1879, finding herself under the weight of a strong displeasure on account of a sister:

«Having to do violence to myself, so that no one might notice my wrenching sorrow, I prove — as I see that it appears — to have changed character. I do not notice it, but they tell me so. And yet my God gave me an indescribable strength because, while I was either reading or taking a report of what was related to me, which was so wrenching that I felt all my interior as if writhing from the violence, because at that moment I had to make myself seen as indifferent and that all who approached me should not notice my position…» (M 4.5, p. 84).

Such equanimity was then the effect of peace of conscience before God; whoever acts rightly fears nothing. She wrote to Mons. Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte in 1898, after having received the news of the apostolic visit, which was to sadden the last two years of her life: «I am most tranquil and content: so they will see everything better. When no subterfuges are made nothing is feared» (L 2-9-98). The same prelate, who knew her intimately, testified at the Process, being cardinal:

«By character, the Servant of God, as I knew her, was neither lively nor phlegmatic, but calm, of that calm joined to resoluteness and firmness. This firmness was always put to the test through so many difficulties of her life, but these were the cause that this virtue of hers shone even more…» (Summ., p. 32).

She sought to form the sisters in self-mastery and serenity of spirit; she suffered deeply when she was informed that some superior scolded her sisters in an intemperate manner. She recommended to Sister A. Adelaide Pezzoni:

«Try to be seen always of the same mood…; to keep always that bearing and composure, joined with meekness and charity, which are the true portrait of the Daughters of St. Anne» (L 1871, 8-1-1872).

And to Sister A. Francesca Camisa:

«Do everything calmly… I recommend meekness to you, because this is the true character of a daughter of St. Anne» (L 13-3-1870, 13-5-1872).

Moral balance is manifested in two important virtues called «cardinal»: justice and prudence. The sisters speak of the Foundress's sense of justice in the informative processes, highlighting the absence in her of every form of favoritism of persons; on this point she was very demanding with the superiors of the communities; she did not tolerate a discriminatory trait among the sisters.

As regards the human habit of prudence, certainly this does not shine in the way she treated herself: her manner of life was almost a permanent attempt against her health, as we shall see further on. Confessors, physicians and ecclesiastical superiors had to declare themselves defeated before that mystery which upset every norm of discretion. Mons. Granito di Belmonte tried to make her moderate her penances, appealing to the obligation of preserving her health for the service of the Institute; but she answered him that «her penances did not prevent her from attending to her duties». He himself attests:

«And the facts have shown that she was quite right, since she always attended to and discharged her office perfectly and ended her days at an advanced age» (Summ., p. 37).

In 1898, when Mother Rosa's two secretaries had recourse to the Cardinal Protector so that he might dissuade her from the journey to Sicily, he replied: «The pains that the Mother has are not ordinary and, therefore, I do not feel like offering her resistance» (FIOCCHI, II, p. 275).

Rigid and ruthless with herself, she was all concern and solicitude when it came to the possible indiscretions of the others. Sincerity and candor

By nobility of heart and by evangelical rectitude, Rosa Gattorno loved the truth. In all her writings sincerity and frankness stand out, without ambiguous or adulatory formulas. Here is a passage from the letter to Mons. Granito di Belmonte in which she wants to dispel a misunderstanding that arose from a letter received by him:

«Take this of mine as you see fit; you know that I am ignorant as an ass, but practice and what I feel for that gratitude and recognition that I owe you, impels me to speak frankly» (L 22-8-1890).

We have confirmation in the deposition of the same prelate:

«In the dealings I had with the Servant of God I became persuaded that she was completely alien to any artifice, to hiding second intentions; I always knew her frank, upright, loyal» (Summ., p. 39).

And she asked of others the same frankness. To the Princess of Fitalia she wrote in the years in which she already addressed her as «tu»: «Tell me frankly what you think, because so Jesus wants, that frank you must be: Yes/ No! (L 29-5-1893). […]

We know from the depositions of the Processes that «her bearing had nothing artificial or affected, but was simple and unaffected; and she wanted her religious also to be without affectation» (Summ., p. 55).

This quality appears above all in the letters to the sisters, especially if they are superiors. Rude, strong expressions suddenly leap out, regarding some sisters, explicable only by the guarantee of the addressee's secrecy: «heads without brains», «bizarre heads», «odd», «frivolous», «little heads»; «that ugly devil of a woman», «that ignorant superior», «wretches», «little beasts», «villains», «vipers». Also in her rapid notes, during visits to the communities, similar expressions are found.

The second of the censors of the writings, after having reported a long list of such outbursts, saw in it nothing that could obscure the heroicity of the virtues of the Servant of God, taking into account her lively way of writing and, above all, the context in which each expression was written. Mother Rosa, moreover, did not take care to leave behind her a reputation for conventional holiness, but to be loyal with herself and with God. Her letters are the best answer to the possible suspicion of pseudo-mystical attitudes in her behavior. […]

Objectivity and practical sense

As a young woman, living in her father's house, she had shown a special aptitude and rare perspicacity in administrative matters, so that the running of the household was almost entirely entrusted to her. Such a capacity, developed later with successive responsibilities, shows itself in so many of her undertakings as foundress, in a special way in the new foundations, in the instructions to the superiors and to other persons. See, as an example, two of the letters written to Mons. Granito di Belmonte on how to meet the expenses of two new houses (16-9-1891, 15-1-1892). Francesco Gattorno, who had the direction of the construction of the Generalate House in Rome, testifies:

«My sister showed in all this administration an extraordinary activity and uncommon intuition. When I went to her for these matters, ordinarily she had already established in her mind the plans to follow, which I, as a man of commerce, found well made» (Summ., p. 647).

And she wanted the sisters to acquire the realistic sense of life, without daydreams or overly angelic attitudes. Here is how she writes to two superiors:

«My daughter, for charity's sake, do not let yourself be taken by fussiness and vague ideas, all things that muddle the mind and serve nothing but to disturb and make us irascible: let us hold to the positive!» (To Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, 16-1-1870) - «You know? I am a positive woman: so I like the daughters of St. Anne to be» (To Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, 20-12-1880).

Certainly, a style of sister such as the foundress wanted it did not become easy: on the one hand separated from the world, immersed in supernatural realities, always recollected and attentive to the presence of God, and on the other with eyes open to temporal realities, objective and practical: the mind in heaven and the feet on earth. Cheerful spirit and sense of humor

We have spoken of a pedagogy of courage; I think that in Mother Rosa's formative methods there is also a notable pedagogy of joy, an essential component of genuine Christian holiness, one of the fruits of the dwelling of the Holy Spirit in us.

By nature, Rosa Gattorno was jovial and communicative. As a young woman she took part in the legitimate amusements of the family circle, bringing her skill in singing and the piano, and did not refuse to accept some turn of the dance, for which later she would feel remorse as for an infidelity to God; passing one day along Via di S. Rocchino, in Genoa, she stopped before a house, inhabited for some time by the Daughters of St. Anne, and looking at it sadly said to a priest: «How many dances I danced in this house!». All her acquaintances, however, remembered her as a girl, cheerful indeed, but most modest and angelic (FIOCCHI, I, p. 17).

The secret of «perfect joy» she had learned in the school of Francis of Assisi, discovering it precisely in scorn and adversities. She wrote, in confidence, to Sister A. Francesca Camisa:

«Little daughter, courage! for to die upon the cross strength and resignation are needed. I have no rest by day or by night: always at the table writing from morning to evening, thoughts upon thoughts, labors upon labors, from all sides I find cruel thorns… but always cheerful and always resigned: so my Jesus teaches me» (13-3-1872).

It was her teaching to the sisters, as appears repeatedly in the letters:

«You will tell all my daughters to be cheerful, as their Mother is» «Cheerful, my little daughter, if you want to become a saint!» - «My dear, cheerful! do you understand?» - «Why are you crying? That is for babies. Come! be cheerful!» - «Be cheerful, and live!» - «Be cheerful! all the rest we shall put in the heart of God the Father» - «As much in prosperity as in adversity, always glad; because in adversity all the more we are to be content, because we know that in rejoicing we give pleasure to our Lord. What greater consolation can we seek than that of pleasing our Jesus?» - «Always cheerful, for so God wills!» - «Trust in God and you will have everything; be cheerful with Jesus: yes, my little daughter, when we have with us the eternal God, what more do we lack? Nothing, nothing!».

And here are some beautiful expressions chosen from the letters to the Princess of Fitalia, inclined to discouragement:

«I see you a little worried: no! I want you cheerful, content! God is with you: whoever has God with him can fear nothing» - «Do not let yourselves be dominated by melancholy. Do you know? This is the net that the devil spreads for good souls… So, away with melancholy! it is a traitor in every extent» - «See, I am cheerful as I can be, tranquil and happy to be able to do for my Jesus some small thing» - «You are in the country: enjoy yourselves, keep the prince cheerful, do not be disturbed if you cannot recollect yourselves: Jesus is content with the desire… Make your offering of the day, that all may be done to the glory of God: eating, drinking, laughing, strolling…» - «I am wretched and good for nothing… Patience! Cheerfulness! May Jesus accept my miserable sufferings» […].

The sense of humor is considered by psychologists as one of the signs of personal integrity and maturity. Psychopathic, neurotic, fanatical or pseudo-mystical individuals do not grasp the optimistic dimension of life, which expresses itself in the art of looking at the facts and attitudes of persons in a humorous key, without dramatizing about the apprehensions of one's own self. «Lord — prayed St. Thomas More —, do not let me worry too much about this embarrassing thing that is the self: Lord, give me a sense of humor».

Mother Rosa offers us also this verification of her human and spiritual normality. A spontaneous and delicate humor imparts to her letters a certain human climate, which is also discovered in her brief notes during the visits to the houses. There is humor also when she speaks of herself to humble herself and when she jokes about her own defects or the ailments of old age. Exquisitely feminine sensibility

Rosa Gattorno possessed in eminent degree the treasure that, humanly, best characterizes the normal woman: the capacity to tune in with what is good, beautiful, pleasant in life and to shun what is morally deformed or unworthy; the gift of intuiting the intimate situations of persons and of feeling close to those who suffer; the sense of detail… When such a treasure is translated into gift of herself, we have the ideal image of the wife and mother of a family, who lives wholly for her own, or that instead of the consecrated woman who immolates herself for God and for others under the impulse of love.

Mother Rosa was a woman of delicately sensitive heart. Here too it is her letters that offer us the most eloquent testimony. She always has present the person of the addressee, with his or her peculiarities, beginning with the name, which she knows how to interject very opportunely in order to reach the heart, with the state of health, with the problems. She worries, like the most solicitous mother, whether the sisters and the girls entrusted to them have enough food, whether they are sheltered from the cold… Let a few of the recommendations to the superiors suffice as an example:

«How it grieves me to hear that you are cold! My Jesus, give them your fire, so they will be sheltered. Dear Francesca, it seems to me that they were all quilted blankets; if you lack them, tell the steward… Tell the steward also to provide you with winter clothes, little jackets, as we agreed, and blankets. For charity's sake, cover yourselves!» - «Console poor little Carlotta, take care of her and have compassion… I recommend the little girls to you and that you see that they are well sheltered at night, so that they do not catch a cough; so too the little ones, the head clean…» (Letters to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 10-10-1867, 2-7-1869; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 25-9-1870).

Sensitive to the needs and situations of others, she was equally grateful for the attentions she received both from the sisters and from other persons. Her letters are full of sentiments of gratitude, in terms of great cordiality.

The gift of sensitivity, however, runs the risk of degenerating, either into touchiness, when it closes in the circle of one's own self, or into apprehensiveness, when the spirit loses freedom and breath under the fears that disturb interior peace. Mother Rosa was exempt from any egocentric withdrawal, but she had to struggle against the second risk, that is, apprehensiveness. She writes in her Memoirs in 1873:

«How much my wretched character makes me suffer! Because ever more I feel torment at the mere thought of having to say a single word of what happens to me. I try everything to amend myself of it, but it is useless, worse! I renew the thought, behold a strong pain awakens in me… It is true that, when this apprehension increases to the point of making me despair, my God comes to my aid, and in peace I remain» (M 4.2, p. 65)!

In similar form she acknowledges it in the book Labors and Consolations, in a supposed dialogue with a «worker» (sister): «I must confess to you that it is my wretched character» (TC, p. 277).

The worst was when such a propensity infiltrated the secret of the spiritual experiences themselves, as one of the most painful factors of the passive purifications. In 1889 she confided in these terms to Mons. Granito di Belmonte:

«Hell, that is, meditating on what swallows up of souls, no, my God! I will only tell him that this meditation was forbidden me by my first confessor. Tender affectionateness, but free from sentimental subjections

In her youthful years, before and after marriage, Rosa won the affection of many persons of Genoese society, because of her delicate and courteous manner and her noble rectitude. It was not difficult for her to find friends and collaborators when, having become a widow, she gave herself to initiatives of piety and charity; indeed, a good number of those friends entrusted themselves fully to her guidance in the ways of the spirit. Later other persons will experience the strong attraction of her heart, always sociable and affectionate, even in the sobriety of her social relations, for which she had no time.

Among all the friendships, none was so deep and intimate as that maintained with Emilia Labecka, Polish by birth, married to Prince Gerolamo Settimo di Fitalia (Palermo). A woman of true spiritual experience, she not only became an admirer and generous benefactress of Mother Rosa's work, but her confidante and true spiritual daughter. The long correspondence kept with the princess until her last illness is a model of cordiality between two souls who have no secrets between them: an affectionate and noble friendship, without affectation. Everything is natural, but everything unfolds on the plane of the interests of the spirit.

The other great friendship was with another personage of the southern nobility, the son of the princes Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, Gennaro, known by her in Naples in 1877, when he was still a layman; he became a priest in 1879, then was attached to the nunciature of Paris (1897), nuncio in Brussels (1899) and in Vienna (1904); finally, in 1911, he was created cardinal by Pius X. He died in 1948.
